usage: to be startled / get a shock
The single most common pairing. 깜짝 almost always attaches to 놀라다.
Said out loud when something startles you. Extremely common spoken reaction.
깜짝 + noun means 'surprise ~'. Also 깜짝 파티 (surprise party), 깜짝 방문 (surprise visit).
Doubled form for repeated startling, e.g. from loud noises.
examples: You called me from behind so suddenly that I got startled.
Classic 깜짝 놀라다 in past tense.
You scared me, when did you come in?
I prepared a surprise party for my friend's birthday.
nuance: 깜짝 captures the instant of being startled, not a slow surprise. By far its strongest collocation is 깜짝 놀라다, and the standalone exclamation 깜짝이야! is something you will hear (and say) constantly in Korea. As a noun-modifier it means 'surprise ~' like 깜짝 세일 or 깜짝 방문.
mistakes: Using 깜짝 alone as a verb. It is an adverb, so you need a verb after it — 깜짝 놀라다, not 깜짝하다 (which is not a real word).
Confusing it with 갑자기 (suddenly). 갑자기 describes timing of any event; 깜짝 is specifically about the startle reaction.

usage: Describes a fast heartbeat from excitement, anticipation, or nervousness.
Used as a verb to describe being excited/nervous. 면접 때문에 두근두근해요.
Pairs naturally with 설레다 (to be thrilled). Positive anticipation.
The verb form 두근거리다 is the more 'literary' single-action equivalent.
examples: It was my first day at work, so my heart was pounding from the morning.
Nervous excitement, very relatable for a newcomer.
When I meet the person I like, my heart pounds.
내일 발표 결과가 나와서 두근두근 떨려요.
The results come out tomorrow, so I'm nervously on edge.
nuance: 두근두근 is the sound-feeling of a racing heart and works for both happy excitement and anxious nerves. It is warmer and more personal than just saying 긴장돼요; Koreans use it for crushes, big days, and anticipation. You can use it adverbially (두근두근 떨려요) or as 두근두근하다.
mistakes: Using it for physical exertion. A pounding heart from running is usually 헐떡거리다 or just 숨차다, not 두근두근.
Forgetting it can be positive. It is not only fear; it heavily implies excitement and 설렘.

usage: The core collocation. Used for stars, clean surfaces, jewelry, eyes.
Adjective-like verb form. 청소했더니 바닥이 반짝반짝해요.
Describes bright, eager eyes, often a child's or someone excited.
Single 반짝 means 'brief flash', as in 반짝 세일 (a short, sudden sale).
examples: The stars are twinkling in the night sky.
After finishing the dishes, the bowls are sparkling clean.
The child waits for the present with sparkling eyes.
nuance: 반짝반짝 evokes light bouncing off something repeatedly: stars, polished floors, jewelry, or bright eager eyes. It is the word in the Korean version of 'Twinkle Twinkle Little Star' (반짝반짝 작은 별). Note the single 반짝 separately means a brief one-off flash, which is why 반짝 세일 means a flash sale.
mistakes: Using it for steady, non-glittering brightness like a lamp. For plain brightness use 밝다, not 반짝반짝.
Mixing up 반짝 (brief flash / sparkle) with 번쩍 (a sudden big flash, like lightning) — 번쩍 is bigger and more startling.

usage: The default collocation. Steady, heavy streaming rain.
비가 주룩주룩 내려요 is the full natural phrase.
Also used for tears running down the face.
For sweat streaming, e.g. in summer heat.
examples: 아침부터 비가 주룩주룩 내려서 우산을 챙겼어요.
It's been pouring since morning, so I grabbed an umbrella.
슬픈 영화를 보다가 눈물이 주룩주룩 흘렀어요.
While watching the sad movie, tears streamed down.
한여름이라 조금만 걸어도 땀이 주룩주룩 나요.
It's midsummer, so I sweat buckets even after walking a little.
nuance: 주룩주룩 describes liquid running down in steady streams — most often heavy rain, but also tears and sweat. It is heavier and more continuous than a light drizzle. For Korea's rainy 장마 season this is the go-to word; you will see it in weather chat and texts constantly.
mistakes: Using it for light rain. Drizzle is 부슬부슬 or 보슬보슬; 주룩주룩 is genuinely heavy, streaming rain.
Pairing it with 오다 awkwardly — 비가 주룩주룩 내리다/와요 are both fine, but 내리다 sounds the most natural.

usage: Big, fast snowfall. 눈이 펑펑 와요.
To splurge / blow money. Slightly disapproving.
Single 펑 is the bursting/popping sound itself (balloon, firework).
examples: After breaking up, I cried my eyes out at home.
밤새 눈이 펑펑 와서 길이 하얘졌어요.
It snowed heavily all night, so the roads turned white.
월급 받자마자 돈을 펑펑 쓰면 안 돼요.
You shouldn't blow your money the moment you get your paycheck.
nuance: 펑펑 has three everyday senses tied by the idea of bursting out abundantly: crying hard (펑펑 울다), heavy snow (눈이 펑펑 와요), and splurging money (돈을 펑펑 쓰다). Context makes the meaning obvious. The single 펑 is the actual 'pop/bang' sound of something bursting.
mistakes: Using 펑펑 for rain. Heavy rain is 주룩주룩 or 쏟아지다; 펑펑 with weather specifically means snow.
Assuming 펑펑 울다 is mild. It implies serious, hard sobbing, not a few tears.

usage: Core usage. Moving quietly so as not to be noticed.
Approaching quietly, often to surprise someone or a pet.
Entering quietly, e.g. coming home late.
examples: 아기가 자고 있어서 살금살금 걸어 나왔어요.
The baby was sleeping, so I tiptoed out.
The cat crept up toward the bird.
I came home late, so I sneaked quietly to my room.
nuance: 살금살금 describes moving deliberately and quietly to avoid being noticed — tiptoeing past a sleeping roommate, a cat stalking, sneaking home late. It carries a slightly playful, cautious feel. It pairs with verbs of motion like 걷다, 다가가다, 들어가다.
mistakes: Confusing it with 슬금슬금, which implies sneaking away gradually/sheepishly (often to avoid blame). 살금살금 is more about quiet footsteps.
Using it for fast quiet movement. Stealthy-but-quick is 후다닥 or 잽싸게; 살금살금 is slow and careful.

usage: Springing up fast, e.g. when you oversleep.
to get ready in a rush
examples: I overslept, so I got ready in a mad rush and left.
배가 너무 고파서 밥을 후다닥 먹었어요.
I was so hungry that I wolfed down my food.
I saw a cockroach and bolted.
Sudden quick escape, a bit comic.
nuance: 후다닥 conveys doing something in a fast, slightly frantic burst — jumping up, rushing to get ready, dashing off. It implies speed plus a bit of commotion or panic, unlike calm efficiency. Great for describing oversleeping mornings, which every newcomer will relate to.
mistakes: Using it for calm, smooth speed. Efficient quickness is 빨리 or 잽싸게; 후다닥 implies a flustered scramble.
Pairing it with slow, deliberate actions — it clashes with verbs like 천천히 or careful tasks.

usage: Shorter 빙빙 is a near-synonym, slightly faster/looser feel.
examples: At the amusement park the carousel spins round and round.
I stood up suddenly and my head started spinning.
The puppy spins in circles chasing its tail.
nuance: 빙글빙글 describes a smooth, continuous spinning in circles — a carousel, a spinning top, or a dizzy head. For dizziness, 머리가 빙글빙글 돌아요 is the natural everyday phrase you'd tell a doctor or friend. The shorter 빙빙 is interchangeable in most cases.
mistakes: Using it for a single half-turn. One turn is 돌다 alone; 빙글빙글 implies repeated, continuous rotation.
Confusing it with 데굴데굴 (rolling like a ball). 빙글빙글 is rotating in place; 데굴데굴 is rolling along the ground.

usage: Light spoken form, often about a child. Written as one word.
Single 콜록 is one cough sound.
examples: I caught a cold and coughed all night long.
Cold symptom, very practical at the pharmacy or clinic.
I kept coughing because of the dust.
Cause of coughing with 거리다 form.
The person next to me kept coughing, so it bothered me.
nuance: 콜록콜록 is the onomatopoeia for repeated coughing and pairs naturally with 기침하다 or stands alone as 콜록콜록거리다. It is the word you'll use to describe cold symptoms to a 약사 (pharmacist) or doctor. A single dry cough is 콜록; the doubled form means ongoing coughing fits.
mistakes: Confusing it with 콜록 vs 쿨럭 — both exist, but 콜록콜록 is the standard, most common spelling for coughing.
Using it for sneezing. A sneeze is 에취 / 재채기; 콜록콜록 is specifically coughing.

usage: Verb form, sometimes implying light snoring.
Progressive: someone is sound asleep right now.
examples: He must have been tired — he's fast asleep on the sofa.
On weekends I want to sleep in soundly until late.
The puppy is sleeping soundly with its belly up.
nuance: 쿨쿨 is the cozy onomatopoeia for sleeping deeply and soundly, the Korean equivalent of 'zzz'. It pairs almost exclusively with 자다 and friends. It has a warm, slightly cute tone — you'd use it for a tired roommate napping or a pet snoozing, not for a formal medical description of sleep.
mistakes: Using it for a quick nap while awake-ish. A light doze is 꾸벅꾸벅 졸다; 쿨쿨 means genuinely deep sleep.
Confusing it with loud snoring. Heavy snoring is 드르렁드르렁 (or 코를 골다); 쿨쿨 is just sound, peaceful sleep.

usage: Core collocation. Something rolling on the ground.
Often used jokingly for laughing or pain on the floor.
Tenser variant 떼굴떼굴 for heavier/bigger rolling.
examples: The ball fell off the desk and rolled away.
It was so funny I rolled on the floor laughing.
The tangerines spilled out of the bag and rolled around.
nuance: 데굴데굴 describes a round object rolling along a surface — a ball, a dropped tangerine, or a person rolling on the floor. The phrase 데굴데굴 구르다 is also used hyperbolically for laughing hard ('rolling on the floor'). Contrast with 빙글빙글, which is spinning in place rather than rolling along.
mistakes: Confusing it with 빙글빙글 (spinning in place). 데굴데굴 always involves moving along the ground.
Using it for tiny objects. For small things rolling (like beads), 또르르 is more natural; 데굴데굴 fits ball-sized objects.

usage: Verb form. Looking this way and that.
The 거리다 form, very common in writing and speech.
Pairs with 주위 / 사방 (surroundings, all directions).
examples: I got lost, so I looked all around me.
I looked around the cafe searching for my friend.
It was a neighborhood I'd never been to, so I walked looking around.
nuance: 두리번두리번 captures turning your head this way and that to look around — searching for someone, getting your bearings when lost, or taking in a new place. It implies a slightly anxious or curious scanning. The 거리다 form 두리번거리다 is just as common as the doubled adverb.
mistakes: Using it for a single glance. One look is 흘끗 보다 or 쳐다보다; 두리번두리번 implies repeated looking in multiple directions.
Confusing it with 기웃기웃 (peeking/peering into places). 두리번두리번 is broad scanning; 기웃거리다 is nosy peeking.
